analysis.one_liner: Creates a government-run public health insurance plan alongside private plans on the ACA exchanges.
analysis.headline: The public option bill died in committee in the 117th Congress without a hearing or a vote, after drawing one cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have created a health insurance plan run directly by the Department of Health and Human Services and sold on the Affordable Care Act exchanges next to private plans. It would follow the same coverage rules as private plans but pay doctors and hospitals at Medicare rates for its first three years, with doctors and hospitals already in Medicare automatically in the network unless they opted out. The goal was a cheaper plan that would pressure private insurers to lower premiums. The bill got one cosponsor and was never taken up by the House Energy and Commerce Committee, dying when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: People who buy their own coverage on the ACA exchanges would gain a cheaper, government-run plan to choose instead of private insurance. Because the public plan would pay providers at Medicare rates and negotiate drug prices, its premiums were designed to be low, and that price competition was expected to push private insurers to reduce their own premiums. The government would also recoup the $2 billion startup funding over ten years.

how_it_helps.text: It added a government-run plan on the ACA exchanges, giving exchange shoppers a public alternative to private insurers for the first time.

Because HHS would pay providers Medicare rates and use its scale to negotiate drug prices, the plan's premiums were expected to be lower than comparable private plans, pressuring private insurers to compete on price.
Nearly all doctors and hospitals already in Medicare would automatically be in the plan's network unless they opted out, so enrollees would start with broad access to providers.
The bill required the plan to follow the same consumer protections, benefits, and cost-sharing rules as private exchange plans, and set up an ombudsman office for enrollees.

analysis.who_pays: Private health insurers would lose exchange customers to the public plan. Doctors and hospitals would be paid Medicare rates for public option patients for the first three years, generally lower than private insurance rates. Drug makers would face government-negotiated prices for drugs the plan covers. Taxpayers would front $2 billion in startup funding, repaid over ten years.
analysis.who_pays_short: Health insurers, hospitals, and drug makers

drawbacks.text: The bill paid doctors and hospitals at Medicare rates for the first three years, which are typically lower than private insurance rates; providers who objected could opt out, which could limit the network of doctors available to public option enrollees.

Premiums had to fully finance both benefits and administrative costs, with the $2 billion startup appropriation repaid to the Treasury over 10 years, so the plan would not be subsidized by general revenue beyond its startup period.
The public option was only available through the ACA exchanges, so people with employer coverage or Medicaid would not have access to it.
Payment rates and methodologies were insulated from administrative or judicial review, meaning providers and others could not challenge the rates the Secretary set.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit would have been a cheaper, government-run coverage option on the ACA exchanges, with the government's lower payment rates disciplining private premiums and startup costs repaid to the Treasury over ten years [S2][S3]. The main drawbacks are on the supply side: paying providers Medicare rates for three years could squeeze hospitals already on thin margins, and providers who found the rates too low could simply opt out, potentially thinning the public plan's network. Because premiums had to fully cover the plan's own costs, its savings for consumers depended on the government actually being more efficient than private insurers, and the option was available only to exchange shoppers rather than everyone. The bill never advanced far enough for any of these design questions to be examined in a hearing.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, which sent it to the Health Subcommittee, and neither ever took it up before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Peter DeFazio introduced the Public Option Deficit Reduction Act on March 18, 2021, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.
On March 19, 2021, the bill was referred to the Subcommittee on Health; the action history shows no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action at any point afterward.
The bill attracted only one cosponsor over its lifetime, both sponsor and cosponsor being House Democrats.
The 117th Congress ended January 3, 2023, and the bill was never reintroduced in that Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers, hospitals, and drug makers benefit from the bill's death, since no public plan now competes with them on the exchanges. No one acted to stop the bill on the record; it simply never advanced.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Health insurers, hospitals, and drug makers

sides.party_line_note: The bill's only two supporters, its sponsor and its single cosponsor, were House Democrats; no Republican backed it, and with just one cosponsor it never came to a vote in either chamber.

industries.note: The bill would have put an HHS-administered plan, expected to price below private coverage, on the exchanges where these companies sell policies. A cheaper public competitor threatens their exchange enrollment and forces them to compete on price. Its death leaves them as the sole sellers of exchange coverage.

They would have been paid Medicare rates (initially 5% higher for some practitioners), which are generally lower than private insurance rates, and Medicare providers would be in the plan automatically unless they opted out. More patients with coverage could offset lower per-service payments, but the rate pressure cuts against them.

For drugs not covered under Medicare, the Secretary would set prices by negotiation rather than accept list prices, so the government plan would be a powerful low-price negotiator. The bill's death keeps that negotiating leverage out of the exchanges.
